posts.title: Pro breakdown: Kilian Jornet, Western States 100 2025
posts.caption:
Kilian Jornet burned 16,104 kcal at the 2025 Western States 100. He ate 6,720.

A case study measured his race with doubly labelled water (a traceable drink that measures calories burned) and a swallowed temperature sensor. He averaged about 86 g of carbs an hour, peaking at 110 g/h in the last 5 hours, and drank 12.5 L (0.87 L/h) with 18.5 g of sodium. He finished 3rd in 14:19:22, 4.3% lighter. The authors concluded that about 90 g/h was tolerable even in extreme heat.

Limits: n = 1, one race, and a world-class runner whose gut and physiology differ from most of ours. Field data, so the heat and terrain were real but uncontrolled. Jornet is a co-author of the paper.

How many grams of carbs an hour do you take on your longest runs?

Source: Mougin, Jornet Burgada et al. 2026, Journal of Applied Physiology, doi.org/10.1152/japplphysiol.01048.2025. Finish from the official Western States 2025 results. Seville average: Jiménez-Alfageme et al. 2025. Raceproof isn't affiliated with Kilian Jornet or Western States.

altText: Pro breakdown, Western States 100. Kilian Jornet burned 16,104 kcal at Western States. He ate 6,720. 3rd in 14:19:22, 2025. Mougin, Jornet Burgada et al. 2026, Journal of Applied Physiology, n = 1.

The test: a real race, 100 miles, extreme heat, mountain terrain. Doubly labelled water (a traceable drink that measures calories burned), a swallowed temperature sensor and kidney blood markers. A research team, with Jornet as a co-author.
Finding 1, energy: he ate less than half of what he burned. Bars: burned 16,104 kcal, ate 6,720 kcal. About 18.8 kcal a minute. n = 1.
Finding 2, carbs: 86 g/h on average, peaking at 110 g/h in the last 5 hours. The authors concluded about 90 g/h was tolerable, even in extreme heat. n = 1.
Finding 3, fluid and sodium: 0.87 L/h, 12.5 L over the race with 18.5 g of sodium. 4.3% body mass lost by the finish. n = 1.
You vs the pro, our take: Seville marathoners averaged 35 g/h. He took 86. Bars: Jornet 86 g/h, guideline up to 90 g/h for races over 2.5 to 3 hours, Seville marathoners 35 g/h.
Test it yourself: take your race fuel on every long run, adding a little each week toward your own race target. Pro numbers are not targets. Raceproof checks: Gut.

Sources and credits: Mougin, Jornet Burgada et al., Journal of Applied Physiology 2026, doi 10.1152/japplphysiol.01048.2025. Finish from official Western States 2025 results. n = 1. Raceproof isn't affiliated with Kilian Jornet, Western States or his sponsors.

posts.title: Research blog: How long does heat acclimation take? (article 2)
posts.caption:
Heat acclimation takes 1 to 2 weeks. The first changes start in 5 days.

In a small trial, 5 days of 90-minute hot rides lowered heart rate 8 bpm and raised plasma volume 7.3%. Sweat runs on its own clock: sodium falls from day 3, sweat rate rises from day 7 to 8. And the gains fade, about 2.5% for every day without heat.

Our take: count heat in days. Aim for 10 to 14 of them, 6 to 2 weeks before your race, then keep 1 or 2 short sessions a week. Heart or blood pressure condition, or pregnant? Talk to your doctor before hot baths or sauna.

Studies: Racinais et al. 2015 (consensus); Tyler et al. 2016 and Daanen et al. 2018 (meta-analyses, mostly lab); Snape et al. 2026 (14 men); Klous et al. 2020 (8 people); Zurawlew et al. 2016 (17 men, controlled trial). Small samples, mostly lab studies.

Full article: raceproof.ai/blog/heat-acclimation-how-long (link in bio). Save this for your next build.

altText: Research blog, heat. Heat acclimation takes 1 to 2 weeks. The first changes start in 5 days. Racinais et al. 2015, Snape et al. 2026. From the Raceproof blog: How long does heat acclimation take?

What the experts say. Plan on 1 to 2 weeks of repeated sessions in the heat (Racinais et al. 2015, consensus of 17 authors). Biggest gains after 14 days; most blocks ran 7 to 14 days (Tyler et al. 2016, meta-analysis of 96 articles).
Within days. 5 days of hot rides, 90 minutes each: heart rate down 8 bpm, plasma volume up 7.3%. Snape et al. 2026, 14 trained men, 7 per group, lab trial.
Sweat has its own clock. A day 1 to 10 timeline: day 3 sweat sodium starts to fall, day 7 to 8 sweat rate starts to rise, day 10 arm sweat rate up 58%. Klous et al. 2020, 8 people, lab.

Hot baths count. 6 days of 40-minute hot baths after easy runs: 5 km time trial in 33°C 4.9% faster, no change at 18°C. Zurawlew et al. 2016, 17 men, controlled trial. Talk to your doctor first if you have a heart or blood pressure condition or are pregnant.
It fades. 2.5% of the gains lost for every day without heat (Daanen et al. 2018). Timeline from 16 weeks out to race day: build heat 6 to 2 weeks out, then keep it. General guideline.

Our take, not a finding of the studies: count heat in days. Aim for 10 to 14 heat days, 6 to 2 weeks before your race, then 1 or 2 short sessions a week. Example card: Heat, 9 runs above 80°F, Ready. Raceproof checks: Heat. Full article on raceproof.ai.

posts.title: Race breakdown: IRONMAN 70.3 Panama (carousel)
posts.caption:
Panama's water was 78°F in 2026, above the 76.1°F age-group wetsuit cutoff. Plan for a swim without a wetsuit.

113.1 km (70.3 mi) with about 463 m of gain and 457 m of loss (approximate), a typical high of 32.0°C and water around 26°C. The next race is Feb 28, 2027, about 17 weeks out.

When to start, counted back from race day: open-water swims from Nov 8, gut training from Dec 6, heat sessions Jan 17 to Feb 14, a weigh-in in race-like heat around Jan 31 to Feb 7, then a 10 to 14 day taper. General guidelines, not a prescription. The taper length comes from coaches, not studies. Never swim open water alone.

Wetsuit figure: Quagliarotti 2021 (up to 11%, mostly pool studies). Open-water plan: Hayes, 220 Triathlon 2026. Raceproof isn't affiliated with IRONMAN or the race.

posts.title: Education: Heat timing (adaptation windows)
posts.caption:
Heat training 20 weeks out is wasted.

Heat adaptation builds over about 10 to 14 days of regular sessions, and it fades without exposure: about 2.5% of the heart rate and core temperature gains for every day without heat (Daanen 2018). So timing matters as much as the work. Build it 6 to 2 weeks before a hot race, then keep 1 or 2 short sessions a week.

Why bother: across 7 marathons, top men finished 1.7% off the course record in the coolest races and 4.5% off in the hottest, and slower runners lost more (Ely et al. 2007, observational).

General guidelines, not a prescription. Heart condition, pregnant or on medication that affects heat tolerance? Talk to your doctor first.

Studies: Ely et al. 2007; Daanen et al. 2018 and Tyler et al. 2016 (meta-analyses, mostly lab studies).

Save this for your next build.

#raceproof #heattraining #marathontraining #triathlontraining #raceprep
altText: Education, heat, adaptation windows. Heat training 20 weeks out is wasted. It builds in about two weeks and fades in a few. When you do it matters as much as how much.
Why it matters: how far top men finished off the course record. Coolest marathons 1.7%, hottest marathons 4.5%. Slower runners lost more as it warmed up. Ely et al. 2007, 7 marathons, observational.

It builds fast: about 10 to 14 days of regular heat sessions. 5 or more days of heat start to adapt heart rate and core temperature. 7 to 14 days is the most common block; longer ones worked better. Daanen et al. 2018, Tyler et al. 2016.
And fades: 2.5% of heart rate and core temperature gains lost per day without heat. Getting it back is 8 to 12 times faster than the first time, so short top-ups keep most of it. Daanen et al. 2018.

Too early, too late, just right, on a timeline from 20 weeks out to race day. 20 weeks out: too early, faded long before race day. Race week: too late, no time for 10 to 14 days of sessions. 6 to 2 weeks out: just right, build it then keep 1 or 2 short sessions a week.

Our take: count back from race day, then start the heat. Raceproof schedules each adaptation in its own window. Talk to your doctor first if you have a heart condition, are pregnant or take medication that affects heat. Example card: Heat, 3 heat sessions done, Building. Raceproof checks: Heat. Save this for your next build.
flags: 8 to 12x faster re-acclimation and "short top-ups keep most of it" come from the Adaptation rates tab (Heat row, citing Daanen 2018); the Research library row for Daanen does not list the 8 to 12x figure.

reels.title: Race breakdown: Black Canyon 100K (v2: intro, when to start, descent deep dive)
reels.caption:
Black Canyon 100K, 2024: overnight snow delayed the desert start to 9:30 am.

100.1 km (62.2 mi) with about 1,591 m of climbing, 2,236 m of descent and a typical high of 17.2°C. The next race is Feb 13, 2027, about 15 weeks out.

The key pillar is descent: about 22 m down for every km. Carry that ratio in your long runs, add 10% a week or less from Nov 21, and fit in 1 to 2 steep downhill sessions a week from Jan 9 to 23. New to steep downhills? Start with relaxed downhills inside your long runs.

General guidelines from coaching sources (Roche, Koop) and Byrnes 1985, not a prescription. Raceproof isn't affiliated with the race.

Full breakdown: raceproof.ai/races/black-canyon-100k (link in bio).
